questions.scenario: A platform lead documented the team's coding conventions (naming, error-handling patterns, review expectations) in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on their own laptop. The conventions work perfectly for the lead, but when teammates clone the repository, Claude Code never follows any of them, and each new hire has to be coached manually.
questions.stem: With minimal ongoing effort, which change makes the conventions apply for everyone who works in the repository?

options.text: Move the conventions into the project-level CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md) and commit it to the repository.
Have each teammate copy the conventions into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md during onboarding.
Commit the conventions into the repository as a docs/conventions.md reference so the content ships with the code for anyone to read.
Record the conventions in each developer's .claude/settings.local.json so they load with the session.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) applies only to that one person across all their projects and is never distributed through version control. The project CLAUDE.md is the team channel: committed to git, it loads for everyone who opens the repository, giving a single shared source of truth with no per-person maintenance.

whyWrong.B: Manual copying multiplies copies that drift out of sync the first time the conventions change, and new hires can be missed.
whyWrong.C: Claude Code loads memory only from its documented locations; a reference file under docs/ never reaches sessions, so committing it changes nothing for Claude even though the content is in git.
whyWrong.D: settings.local.json holds structured settings and permission rules, not freeform prose conventions, and it is personal to one machine anyway.

questions.mindset: Team conventions travel through git at project scope, not through anyone's home directory.

questions.scenario: A tech lead tuned the team's Claude Code runs by setting the `model` key in their own `.claude/settings.local.json`, which is not committed to the shared repository. On the lead's machine everything runs with the intended model, but teammates who clone the repo get a different model, so review quality and cost differ per machine.
questions.stem: What is the best fix for a model setting that must be consistent across the whole team?

options.text: Ask every teammate to set the same model in their ~/.claude/settings.json during setup.
Move the model setting into the committed project .claude/settings.json, keeping local settings for personal overrides only.
Commit .claude/settings.local.json to the repository so all machines read the same file.
Document the required model in CLAUDE.md and rely on Claude to use it when working.

questions.explanation: Settings precedence runs managed > command line > local > project > user. `settings.local.json` overrides the project file but is personal and kept out of git (Claude even auto-adds it to excludes), which is exactly why the lead's choice never reached anyone else. Team-wide standards belong in the committed project `.claude/settings.json`; local and user files remain the right place for individual overrides.

whyWrong.A: Per-user settings are set machine by machine and drift as soon as anyone forgets or changes them; there is no shared source of truth.
whyWrong.C: settings.local.json is the personal layer (it also collects each developer's own approval rules); committing it both fights the tooling and mixes private state into shared config.
whyWrong.D: CLAUDE.md is guidance injected as context; it does not configure which model runs, so behavior stays uncontrolled.

questions.mindset: Match the settings file to the audience: shared layer for shared standards, local layer for personal tweaks.

questions.scenario: A security team requires that no developer workstation, CI runner, or contractor laptop be able to re-enable a capability the organization has disabled in Claude Code — not by editing project files, not by user settings, and not by passing command-line flags.
questions.stem: Which configuration mechanism satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Add the policy to every repository's committed .claude/settings.json and review repos periodically.
Add the policy to each user's ~/.claude/settings.json and communicate that it must not be changed.
State the policy in the organization's CLAUDE.md guidance so Claude refuses to help bypass it.
Deploy the policy through managed-settings.json on all organization-managed machines.

questions.explanation: Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence chain (managed > command line > local > project > user) and cannot be overridden by any lower scope, including CLI arguments. This is the only layer where an organization-wide, non-overridable control belongs. Project and user files can always be edited by the people they apply to, and CLAUDE.md is guidance for the model, not an enforced configuration boundary.

whyWrong.A: Project settings rank below local settings and command-line flags, so anyone working in the repo can override the policy on their own machine; periodic review does not make the rule binding.
whyWrong.B: User settings are entirely under each person's control; a request not to change them is a policy hope, not a control.
whyWrong.C: CLAUDE.md is context that shapes model behavior probabilistically; it cannot disable a tool, mode, or capability, and it governs the model rather than the configuration layers.

questions.mindset: Non-overridable policy lives in managed settings; everything below it is negotiable by definition.

questions.scenario: A team's automated review workflow sets `model` to the alias `sonnet` in Claude Code settings. Nothing in the repository changed, yet after a model release the workflow's output style and token costs shifted noticeably, and two review checks started failing intermittently.
questions.stem: With minimal ongoing effort, how should the team keep model behavior stable in this workflow?

options.text: Keep the alias but add a note in the settings file documenting the model release the team validated against.
Switch the alias to `opus` instead, betting that a different tier's release cadence disrupts their workload less.
Replace the alias with the full model ID, a pinned snapshot that only changes when the team deliberately updates it.
Move the sonnet alias from project settings into ~/.claude/settings.json so it is configured once per machine.

questions.explanation: Aliases like `sonnet`, `opus`, and `haiku` are pointers that move to the newest release of their tier, so behavior can change without any config edit. A full model ID identifies a specific snapshot, so the workflow runs the same model until the team deliberately evaluates a successor and updates the ID. This turns model changes into reviewed, planned events rather than silent shifts.

whyWrong.A: A note documents intent but has no effect on resolution; the alias still silently moves to the new release.
whyWrong.B: Every alias tracks the newest release of its tier; switching tiers changes capability and cost without adding stability.
whyWrong.D: The file's location is irrelevant — an alias resolves to the latest release whether it is set in project, local, or user settings.

questions.mindset: Aliases are moving pointers; pinned full model IDs are the stability mechanism.

questions.scenario: A customer-support summarization feature regressed last week. The prompts live in a shared document that several engineers edit directly, and production logs record only the request and response text. The team cannot determine which prompt revision, combined with which model, produced the traffic that customers complained about, so they cannot reproduce or fix the regression confidently.
questions.stem: Which practice best prevents this situation from recurring?

options.text: Store prompts in version control, gate tagged releases on eval results, and log the prompt version and model ID with each request.
Log the complete prompt text alongside every request and response so any past call can be read in full.
Instruct the model to begin each response by stating which instructions it followed, and log that statement.
Freeze all prompt edits until a quarterly release window so there are fewer revisions to disambiguate.

questions.explanation: Prompts and model IDs are release artifacts, just like code. Versioning prompts in git, gating changes on evals, and recording the prompt version plus model ID per request makes every past behavior attributable and reproducible: any complaint maps to an exact (prompt version, model ID) pair that can be re-run and compared.

whyWrong.B: Full-text logging is expensive, may capture sensitive content, and still doesn't tie behavior to an eval-gated, tagged release — you can read the text but not reconstruct the change history or validation state.
whyWrong.C: The model's self-report about which instructions it followed is unreliable output, not an audit record of which prompt version was actually sent.
whyWrong.D: Slowing down edits doesn't create version identity; the next incident still can't be traced to a specific revision.

questions.mindset: If you can't name the (prompt version, model ID) pair behind a request, you can't debug production behavior.

questions.scenario: A team installed a plugin from a marketplace for a release-notes workflow without constraining its version. The plugin's author shipped an update overnight; the workflow's slash command now behaves differently and the pipeline that depends on it broke, even though the team changed nothing.
questions.stem: What should the team do at installation time to prevent silent behavior changes like this?

options.text: Disable the plugin whenever it is not actively in use and re-enable it for each run.
Ask the plugin author to announce breaking changes in advance and watch the announcements.
Copy the plugin's instructions into CLAUDE.md so the workflow no longer depends on the plugin.
Constrain the plugin dependency to the version range the team tested, and re-test before adopting newer releases.

questions.explanation: An unconstrained dependency tracks the latest release, so the author's overnight update flowed straight into the team's environment. Constrain plugin dependencies to the version range the team tested, so updates arrive only as deliberate, re-tested upgrades — the same discipline applied to any other dependency in the stack.

whyWrong.A: Toggling the plugin on and off changes nothing about which version resolves when it is enabled, and adds operational friction.
whyWrong.B: Relying on the author's communication habits is not a control; the update ships regardless of announcements.
whyWrong.C: Forking the behavior into CLAUDE.md abandons the plugin's maintained implementation, duplicates logic, and drifts from the source.

questions.mindset: Treat plugin versions like library dependencies: unconstrained means the author deploys to your pipeline.

questions.scenario: A team wants every developer's Claude Code sessions to connect to an internal MCP server that exposes their deployment tools. The server requires a per-developer API token. The repository is shared across the team, and the security policy forbids tokens in git.
questions.stem: Which configuration approach shares the server definition through the repository without committing secrets?

options.text: Each developer runs the add command at local scope with their token inline, keeping the server in their own private config.
Commit a project .mcp.json at the repo root that references the token through environment variable expansion, with each developer exporting their own token.
Put the token in an environment key inside .claude/settings.json and commit that file so everyone shares it.
Paste the token into CLAUDE.md so it is available on every surface that reads project instructions.

questions.explanation: A project-scoped `.mcp.json` at the repository root is the team-shared MCP configuration channel: committed to git, it reaches everyone who clones the repo. It supports environment variable expansion (e.g. `${INTERNAL_TOKEN}` with an optional default), so the shared file carries the server definition while each developer's secret stays in their local environment. Project-scoped servers prompt for approval on first use, which is the intended trust step.

whyWrong.A: Local scope config is private per project and machine; nothing flows through the repository, so every setup is a manual, drifting re-implementation.
whyWrong.C: That commits the token itself to version control — exactly what the security policy forbids.
whyWrong.D: CLAUDE.md is model-facing context; placing a live credential there exposes the secret to every prompt and has nothing to do with MCP server configuration.

questions.mindset: Share the config through git, share nothing sensitive — environment expansion is the bridge.

questions.scenario: An internal audit requires that a destructive shell-command pattern never executes in the team's automated Claude Code runs. The team wrote 'never run destructive cleanup or force-push commands' prominently in the project CLAUDE.md. The audit's sample still found instances where the commands ran during long autonomous sessions.
questions.stem: What is the most reliable change the team can make?

options.text: Strengthen the CLAUDE.md wording and add explicit examples of every forbidden command variant.
Instruct Claude to verify each command against the policy before running it and to skip disallowed ones.
Add permission deny rules (and, where ordering matters, a PreToolUse hook) so the blocked commands are refused before execution.
Run the automated sessions on a more instruction-following model tier so the rule is respected more often.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is context delivered to the model — guidance with a non-zero failure rate, especially in long sessions where instructions can lose salience. Permissions and hooks are enforced by Claude Code itself, deterministically, before the tool runs: deny rules are evaluated ahead of allow rules and apply in every permission mode, including bypass. Guarantees belong in enforcement layers; CLAUDE.md remains useful as supporting guidance.

whyWrong.A: More emphatic wording with more examples is still probabilistic; audit findings will continue at a lower but nonzero rate.
whyWrong.B: Asking the model to police itself is the same probabilistic channel as the original rule — self-checks fail exactly when the model is already off track.
whyWrong.D: A more capable model shifts the failure rate but the control still depends on model judgment; the requirement is 'never', which only an enforced boundary delivers.

questions.mindset: 'Must never happen' is a permissions/hooks question, never a CLAUDE.md question.

questions.scenario: A repository's root CLAUDE.md has grown to 600 lines, mixing universal conventions with detailed rules that only apply to API-client files that are scattered across many service directories. A developer split the file into modular pieces referenced with @path imports, expecting smaller per-session token usage, but every session still loads the same content and the context cost is unchanged.
questions.stem: Why did the refactor not help, and what would genuinely reduce always-loaded context?

options.text: The split files were still too large; breaking them under 200 lines each will make sessions load only the pieces they reference.
Duplicating the client rules into a CLAUDE.md inside every service directory ensures only the active directory's file is loaded.
Imports all load at launch; keep universal conventions in the root file and move the scattered, path-specific rules into .claude/rules/ files with paths globs that load when matching files are read.
Raise the @import recursion depth so deeply nested files load lazily only when something references them.

questions.explanation: @imports are an organization mechanism, not a loading optimization: imported files load at launch just like inline text, so splitting changed nothing. The on-demand mechanisms are path-scoped rules (`.claude/rules/` with `paths` globs, which load when Claude reads a matching file — ideal for conventions tied to files scattered across directories) and skills, whose full content loads only when invoked. The root file should stay lean and universal.

whyWrong.A: File size isn't the trigger; imports load eagerly regardless of line count, so smaller files still all load at launch.
whyWrong.B: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load only when Claude reads files in that directory, but the rules apply to client files spread across many directories, and duplicating the text per directory guarantees drift — the glob-based rule file is the purpose-built mechanism.
whyWrong.D: Import depth only bounds how many hops an import chain may follow (up to four); there is no lazy loading of imports.

questions.mindset: Imports organize; rules with paths and skills are what actually defer loading.

questions.scenario: A production application pins a dated model ID in code, and its prompts are versioned in git with an eval suite gating every release. The vendor announces that this model will be retired in three months and a successor is already available.
questions.stem: What is the best way for the team to adopt the successor while protecting production behavior?

options.text: Run the existing eval suite against the successor with current prompts, fix regressions, then switch the pinned model ID as a reviewed release.
Update the pinned model ID on the successor's launch day and watch the production quality dashboards for regressions afterwards.
Keep the retired model ID in place indefinitely, since a pinned snapshot continues serving traffic after retirement.
Stop pinning a model ID and request whatever model is newest at call time so no future migration is ever needed.

questions.explanation: Model retirement is a planned lifecycle event: because prompts and model IDs are versioned, gated release artifacts, migration is a reviewed release — run the eval suite against the successor, address regressions (prompt tweaks become versioned changes too), then update the pinned ID with the ability to roll back to the previous pair. This is exactly what pinning and eval gating exist to enable.

whyWrong.B: Monitoring after an unvalidated switch detects regressions in production traffic — the eval suite exists precisely so regressions are caught before customers see them.
whyWrong.C: A retired snapshot stops being served at the retirement date; keeping the ID guarantees an outage, not stability.
whyWrong.D: Always taking the newest model makes behavior change silently with every release and destroys reproducibility of past outputs — the opposite of what pinning provides.

questions.mindset: A model migration is a release: eval first, then switch the pinned artifact deliberately.

questions.scenario: A developer keeps personal preferences in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ('always use tabs; end every task with a chatty summary'). A new repository's committed project CLAUDE.md specifies spaces and terse, structured summaries. The developer expected the project file to replace their personal one, but output formatting flips between the two styles from task to task.
questions.stem: What explains the inconsistency, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The project file does replace the user file, so the flips are ordinary sampling variation; re-running the tasks should settle it.
Memory files are concatenated, not overridden — both rule sets are in context — so the conflicting personal rules should be removed or narrowed in the user file.
Creating a CLAUDE.local.md in the project will override both files and restore consistent formatting.
Settings precedence applies here: moving the personal conventions into ~/.claude/settings.json makes them win over the project file.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md files load broadest-to-most-specific and are concatenated, never replaced: user, project, and local files all contribute text to the same context, with more-specific files simply read later. Two contradictory rule sets therefore stay in context and the model oscillates. The fix is at the source: delete or narrow the conflicting personal rules, keeping user-level memory for preferences that don't fight project standards.

whyWrong.A: Replacement never happens — concatenation is the documented behavior, so the inconsistency is structural, not sampling noise.
whyWrong.C: CLAUDE.local.md is appended after the project file in the same directory; it adds a third instruction source rather than removing the conflict.
whyWrong.D: Settings precedence governs settings keys, not memory text; settings files cannot hold these prose conventions, and user settings rank below project settings anyway.

questions.mindset: Memory files stack, they don't override — resolve conflicts at the source, not by adding more layers.

questions.scenario: A team is standardizing which Claude Code configuration artifacts belong in the repository. Some developers have been committing everything from their working directory, others nothing, and onboarding currently depends on tribal knowledge about which files to copy by hand.
questions.stem: Which TWO artifacts should be committed to the shared repository? Choose TWO.

options.text: Each developer's .claude/settings.local.json, so that everyone's permission approvals are shared with the team.
The shared .claude/settings.json containing the team's permission rules and project standards.
A CLAUDE.local.md with team conventions, so each developer gets the same local overrides.
Developers' ~/.claude/settings.json files, copied into the repo folder for reference.
A project .mcp.json that defines the team's MCP servers, with credentials referenced through environment variable expansion.

questions.explanation: The shared layer of the repository should carry exactly the team-level configuration: the committed project `.claude/settings.json` (team permission rules, standards) and the project `.mcp.json` (team MCP servers), with secrets kept out via `${VAR}` expansion so the file is safe to commit. Personal artifacts — local settings, CLAUDE.local.md, user-scope files — stay on individual machines by design.

whyWrong.A: settings.local.json is the personal layer; it collects private approvals and overrides and is auto-excluded from git. Committing it shares individuals' permissions and clobbers everyone's personal state.
whyWrong.C: CLAUDE.local.md is the personal, this-project-only memory file that belongs in .gitignore; team conventions belong in the project CLAUDE.md.
whyWrong.D: ~/.claude/settings.json is the user scope that lives in each person's home directory across all their projects; a copy in the repo is dead weight that is loaded by no one and immediately drifts.

questions.mindset: Commit the team layer (project settings, .mcp.json with env-var secrets); keep the personal layer out of git.

questions.scenario: A regulated financial product routes loan-document analysis through Claude. Compliance asks the engineering team to guarantee that any output decision from the past can be attributed to the exact prompt and model that produced it, and that prompt changes cannot reach production without evidence they preserve quality.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices satisfy these requirements? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep prompts under version control and require eval results to pass before a new prompt version is released.
Replace identifiers with full-text logging of every prompt and response for every request handled.
Pin the model aliases (such as sonnet and opus) in configuration so the underlying model never changes.
Record the prompt version and the model ID alongside each request in application logs.
Regenerate all historical outputs after every prompt change to confirm that decisions would not have differed.

questions.explanation: Prompts and model IDs are release artifacts. Versioning prompts in git and gating each change on evals gives the evidence trail compliance wants before changes ship; logging the prompt version and model ID per request makes every past decision attributable to an exact, re-runnable (prompt version, model ID) pair. Together they turn 'what produced this output?' into a lookup instead of an investigation.

whyWrong.B: Full-text logging is high-volume and may capture sensitive borrower data, and it still doesn't establish which reviewed, eval-gated version produced behavior — text is not a version identity.
whyWrong.C: Aliases are moving pointers that resolve to the newest release, so pinning an alias does not pin the model; only a full model ID does.
whyWrong.E: Re-running history after each change is enormously costly, is itself a new set of model calls rather than evidence about what shipped, and does nothing to gate changes before release.

questions.mindset: Attribution = version identity in logs; quality = eval gates on release — you need both.

questions.scenario: A team is rolling out Claude Code plugins across the organization. Several developers have begun installing whatever marketplace plugins look useful, and maintainers are worried about both supply-chain risk and the quality of everyday sessions degrading as the plugin set grows.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices should the team adopt? Choose TWO.

options.text: Enable every plugin the marketplace offers so Claude has maximum capability available in every session.
Install plugins at user scope by default so they apply uniformly across all of each developer's projects.
Review what each plugin contains — its skills, hooks, and MCP servers — and what it can do on the machine before installing it.
When a plugin update breaks behavior, patch the installed plugin's files in place until the author fixes it.
Constrain each plugin dependency to the tested version range and re-test before adopting newer releases.

questions.explanation: Plugins bundle executable components — skills, hooks, MCP servers — and they run code as you, so each one deserves a review of its contents and capabilities before installation. And because an unconstrained dependency tracks the latest release, version ranges plus re-testing turn updates from surprise deployments into deliberate upgrades. These two practices cover the risk axis and the change-control axis.

whyWrong.A: Every enabled plugin's skill and agent descriptions consume context in every turn; an unbounded plugin set taxes all sessions and widens the attack surface for no benefit most tasks ever use.
whyWrong.B: User scope is a distribution choice, not a safety measure — it spreads the plugin and its context cost across every project on the machine; scope should match where the plugin is actually needed.
whyWrong.D: Hand-editing installed plugin files creates unmanaged local drift that the next update overwrites; version constraints and upstream fixes are the maintainable path.

questions.mindset: Plugins are executable dependencies: review before install, constrain versions after.

questions.scenario: A security engineer adds a `permissions.deny` rule for a risky command to the committed project `.claude/settings.json`. A developer on the team had earlier clicked 'Yes, don't ask again' for that same command, which saved a matching allow rule in their `.claude/settings.local.json`. The developer believes their local file wins because it has higher precedence.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are correct? Choose TWO.

options.text: The deny rule still applies, because deny rules are evaluated before allow rules regardless of which settings file they come from.
List-valued keys such as permissions.allow merge across settings files, so the developer's local allow entries add to — rather than replace — the project's permission configuration.
The developer's local allow wins because .claude/settings.local.json outranks .claude/settings.json in settings precedence.
Moving the deny rule into the developer's ~/.claude/settings.json would make it impossible to override.
Once developers are trained on the new policy, the deny rule can be removed without changing the security posture.

questions.explanation: Two different mechanisms are in play, and the question conflates them. Precedence (managed > CLI > local > project > user) resolves what a single key's value is; but list-valued keys like `permissions.allow` merge across files rather than replace, and rule evaluation is ordered deny → ask → allow with first match winning. So the local allow rule coexists with the project configuration yet can never defeat the deny — an allow saved at local scope does not outrank deny (or ask) rules from higher scopes.

whyWrong.C: Precedence never lets an allow beat a deny: evaluation order puts deny ahead of allow everywhere, in every permission mode.
whyWrong.D: User settings are the lowest precedence scope; a deny there is still evaluated before allows, but it is the weakest place to put an organizational control — project or managed scope is where shared rules belong.
whyWrong.E: Training is not enforcement: removing the deny leaves the boundary dependent on model and human behavior, which is precisely what the rule exists to avoid.

questions.mindset: Precedence resolves duplicate keys; deny-before-allow evaluation resolves rule conflicts — an allow can never beat a deny.
